name: Nikhil Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at the community health centre on Mill Street by half seven, and the first patient is in at eight whether I've had coffee or not. It's ten-minute slots, about thirty-two people a day: chest infections, diabetes checks, a lot of men from the old mill who've let things go far too long. I like the long-term ones best, the patients I've watched get better over two years. What wears me out is the paperwork after six, the referral letters and the sick notes I type with two fingers.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said the paperwork wears you out. Has the clinic tried any AI tools to help with that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: They're piloting an AI note-taker that listens to the consultation and writes it up. Half the doctors use it; I don't, and I've said so in two staff meetings. I don't want a microphone between me and a frightened patient, and I don't trust where those recordings go. Grace, the practice nurse I have lunch with, thinks I'm being a dinosaur at twenty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now can we talk about the real problem, which is there aren't enough doctors and the waiting list is six weeks. I'd probably post something like that in the union group chat. The tech was never going to fix underfunding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my life stays the same, and the same isn't great. I've got a student loan that takes a big bite every month, rent on the flat went up again in spring, and I have maybe three weeks of money in the bank. The clinic pays less than the private practices because it's public, and there's nowhere else within forty minutes I could go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my list and pick up a couple of Saturday shifts at the urgent-care centre in the next town, because that's the only way I get ahead. I'd keep refusing the note-taker, and nobody would make a fuss if it's only shaving a few minutes. Maybe I'd finally put fifty a month into a savings account instead of telling myself I will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit relieved, a bit flat. Nothing is coming to take my job, but nothing is coming to rescue me either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a couple of Saturday shifts. What would that money actually go to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The loan first, then a proper winter coat, because I've been wearing the same one since medical school. If I'm honest, the Saturday money would mostly vanish into the car, which needs new tyres before the snow. I'd rather do fewer shifts, but the maths doesn't let me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't use the note-taker. In this picture, would anyone push you to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, if it's just a small time saver. The practice manager likes it, but she can't force a doctor to record patients. If the tool turns out to be hype, I'll have been right for once, and Grace will have to buy lunch.

say: The real problem is **too few doctors** and a six-week waiting list, not missing software.
Technology was never going to fix **underfunding** in public clinics.
think: My life stays the same, and the same means a **student loan**, rising rent and three weeks of savings.
The public clinic pays less, and there's **nowhere else** within forty minutes to work.
do: Take **two Saturday shifts** a month at the urgent-care centre in the next town.
Keep **refusing the note-taker** while it stays optional and only saves minutes.
Start putting **fifty a month** into a savings account for the first time.
feel: Relieved that **nothing threatens** the job, but flat because nothing gets easier either.
S0.quote: Nothing is coming to take my job, but nothing is coming to rescue me either.
fieldNote: Even in the calmest picture he carries **real money pressure**: a loan, rising rent and three weeks of savings.
His refusal of the **AI note-taker** is about trust and privacy, not just habit.
He frames everything through **public underfunding**, which he sees as the real threat to his work.

steps.text: Work two Saturday shifts a month at the urgent-care centre
Put fifty a month into a savings account
Keep seeing about thirty-two patients a day on Mill Street

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say out loud that if software writes the letters, the time saved should go to patients, not to squeezing more of them into a day. I'd bring that to the union branch meeting, because I know what management will do. They'll call it efficiency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the clinic would stop replacing doctors who leave. Doctor Okafor retires in two years, and I'd bet they'd cover his list with AI triage and a nurse rather than hire someone. Then my slots go from ten minutes to eight, and if I keep refusing the tools, I'm the slow one they look at first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the union branch to put in writing that the time saved goes to longer appointments. I'd sell the car and take the bus to save the insurance and the tyres, and I'd keep the Saturday shifts going. I'd probably have to use the note-taker in the end, but I'd do it last and complain the whole time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest, honestly. I trained for seven years to listen to people, and I'd be watching a computer get credit for my thinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be the slow one they look at first. What would that look like in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The practice manager prints a sheet every month showing patients seen per doctor. If everyone else is at forty with the software and I'm at thirty-two, that sheet ends up on the partners' table. There's no other clinic nearby, so I can't just walk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about, apart from yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The receptionists, mostly, because answering phones and booking is exactly what this picture takes. Linda on the front desk has been there nineteen years and she knows every family in town. If a booking bot replaces Linda, half our patients will just stop calling.

say: Time saved by **AI letters** should go to patients, not to more appointments per day.
Management will call **squeezing doctors** efficiency, and the union needs to say so first.
think: The clinic would **stop replacing** doctors who leave and cover their lists with AI triage.
If he keeps refusing the tools, he expects to be **first in line** when numbers are compared.
do: Push the **union branch** to get a written promise that saved time means longer appointments.
Sell the **car** and take the bus to cut insurance and repair bills.
Use the note-taker only when **forced**, and keep the Saturday shifts going.
feel: Tight-chested and **resentful** that a computer would get credit for his thinking.
S1.quote: I trained for seven years to listen to people, and I'd be watching a computer get credit for my thinking.
fieldNote: He expects the danger to come through **hiring freezes**, not sudden sackings.
The monthly **patients-per-doctor sheet** is where he imagines his resistance getting punished.
He worries for the **receptionists** more than for himself, especially Linda, nineteen years on the desk.

steps.text: Bring a written promise on appointment length to the union branch
Sell the car and take the bus to the clinic
Keep working Saturday urgent-care shifts for the loan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is reckless and the government should stop it until there are rules about who is responsible when the machine gets a diagnosis wrong. I'd sign every petition going and I'd say it in the union chat, at the pub, everywhere. Patients deserve a person they can hold to account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's simple. By 2028 the thinking half of my job is gone, and nobody pays a doctor's wage for the hands-on half. Working out what's wrong, choosing the drug, writing the letter: the software does all of that faster than me. What's left until about 2031 is listening to a chest and pressing on a belly, and they'll pay a nurse or a health assistant less to do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop pretending and put every spare bit of money toward the loan so it's smaller when the pay drops. I'd go on the union's health committee and lobby our local representative for a law that a doctor signs off every diagnosis. If the clinic cut me back to part time, I'd move back into my parents' spare room in the next town to stop paying rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. I'd lie awake doing sums about the loan, and the sums don't work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years isn't long. What would you do in the first month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cancel everything that isn't food, rent or the loan, which isn't much to begin with. Then I'd ring my mum and tell her I might need the spare room, which would be a hard call to make at twenty-seven. After that, the union meeting, because on my own I'm just one grumpy doctor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're quite set against using AI. If it arrives this fast, would you learn it anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to learn enough to check it, because someone has to catch the mistakes. But I wouldn't throw myself into it the way some of my classmates would. I'd rather spend those two years fighting for the rule that a human signs off.

say: The government should **halt it** until there are rules on blame for wrong diagnoses.
Patients deserve a person they can **hold to account**, and he'd say it everywhere.
think: By 2028 the **thinking half** of his job is gone: diagnosis, prescribing and letters.
The hands-on part left until 2031 won't earn a **doctor's wage**; nurses and assistants will do it cheaper.
do: Put every spare bit of money into **paying down** the student loan.
Join the union's **health committee** and lobby for a doctor to sign off diagnoses.
Move back into his **parents' spare room** if the clinic cuts him to part time.
feel: Physically **sick** and lying awake doing loan sums that don't add up.
S2.quote: By 2028 the thinking half of my job is gone, and nobody pays a doctor's wage for the hands-on half.
fieldNote: He splits his job cleanly into **thinking and hands-on**, and sees only the cheaper half surviving.
Asking his mum for the **spare room** is the part he finds hardest to say.
Even under pressure he'd learn AI only to **check its mistakes**, not to embrace it.

steps.text: Put every spare bit of money toward the student loan
Join the union health committee within the first month
Lobby the local representative for doctor sign-off on diagnoses
Move into his parents' spare room if cut to part time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, but louder and more organised, because five years is long enough to get a law through if people push. I'd say it at the branch meeting: we have a window, let's not waste it. I'd also say it to patients who ask, carefully, because some of them are already scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it buys me time to get the loan down, and that matters a lot. By 2031 the diagnosing and the letters go, and around 2034 the robots could do the examinations too. I'd be thirty-two, still renting, and I don't see myself becoming some kind of tech person at that point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the Saturday shifts every week for three years and clear most of the loan. I'd stand for the union branch committee and help write a proposal for how clinics should use AGI safely. I'd keep doing my list the old way for as long as they let me, because that's the part I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less sick, more grim. Five years feels like knowing the river will flood and spending every weekend building the wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Three years of Saturday shifts is a lot. What gives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My social life, what little there is, and probably my football on Sundays because I'd be too tired. My friends from medical school would see me even less. I'd tell myself it's temporary, which is what doctors always say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep doing your list the old way. What if they insist you use the new system?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd use it, under protest, and I'd write down every mistake it makes. That notebook would go to the union, because evidence beats complaining. I'm stubborn, but I'm not stupid enough to lose the job over it.

say: Five years is a **window** to get a law through if people organise properly.
He'd talk to worried **patients** carefully, because some are already scared.
think: The extra time mostly lets him **shrink the loan** before his pay drops.
At thirty-two, still renting, he doesn't see himself becoming a **tech person**.
do: Work **every Saturday** for three years to clear most of the student loan.
Stand for the union **branch committee** and help draft rules for safe AGI use in clinics.
Keep a **notebook of mistakes** if forced onto the new system, and hand it to the union.
feel: Grim rather than sick, like **building a flood wall** before a known flood.
S3.quote: Five years feels like knowing the river will flood and spending every weekend building the wall.
fieldNote: The extra three years turn his panic into **grim planning**, mostly around debt.
He'd give up his **Sunday football** and friends, calling it temporary, as doctors do.
His resistance shifts into **documenting errors** for the union rather than flat refusal.

steps.text: Work every Saturday urgent-care shift for three years
Clear most of the student loan before 2031
Stand for the union branch committee and draft safe-use rules

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, so there's no excuse for doing it badly. I'd say that in the union newsletter and at the clinic. The question is whether the people in charge use the decade or waste it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years helps me more than anything else in this conversation. I'd be thirty-seven when the thinking work goes, with the loan paid off if I'm careful. But I'd still be a doctor whose whole skill is the thinking work, and I've no idea what I'd be at forty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay off the loan over six or seven years and build three months of savings for the first time in my life. I'd stay in the union and push for a fund that retrains health workers, paid by the companies that sell the AI. I might train in something hands-on, like minor surgery or joint injections, because the robots come later for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can breathe. Ten years is the first picture where I can see myself still standing at the end of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned minor surgery and injections. Is that a real plan or a thought?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Somewhere in between. Doctor Okafor does joint injections and he's offered to teach me twice, and I've said I'm too busy both times. With ten years' warning I'd stop saying that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame, if anyone, for how this goes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the engineers, really. I'd blame governments that let a few companies own the whole thing and keep the money. If AI makes medicine cheaper, that saving should go back into clinics like ours, and I don't trust anyone to do that without being forced.

say: Ten years is enough to do this **properly**, so there's no excuse for doing it badly.
Whether leaders **use the decade** or waste it is the real question.
think: At thirty-seven, with the **loan paid**, he'd be in a much better position.
His whole skill is **thinking work**, and he can't picture what he'd be at forty.
do: Pay off the loan and build **three months of savings** over six or seven years.
Push the union for a **retraining fund** paid by the companies that sell AI.
Let Doctor Okafor teach him **joint injections** and minor procedures.
feel: Uneasy but **able to breathe**, picturing himself still standing at the end.
S4.quote: Ten years is the first picture where I can see myself still standing at the end of it.
fieldNote: Time matters hugely to him because of the **debt**: ten years lets him clear it.
He finally accepts an offer he turned down twice, to learn **hands-on procedures**.
He blames **governments and big companies**, not engineers, and wants savings returned to clinics.

steps.text: Pay off the student loan within seven years
Learn joint injections from the senior partner
Push the union for a retraining fund paid by AI companies

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt, because I'd still have most of the loan and no savings when the thinking part goes. What would help is a law that a qualified doctor signs off every diagnosis, and some breathing room on the loan repayments if my hours get cut. I don't want a handout, I want the time to adjust that the fast one doesn't give me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the patients who don't have smartphones. Half my diabetes list are older men who'd never talk to an app about their feet. If clinics go digital overnight, those men just disappear from the system, and nobody notices until they turn up at hospital with gangrene.

headlineQuote: Half my diabetes list are older men who'd never talk to an app about their feet.
portrait: Nikhil is a **27-year-old** family doctor at a public community clinic on Mill Street in a former mill town.
He carries a **student loan**, rising rent and three weeks of savings, with no other clinic within forty minutes.
He refuses the clinic's **AI note-taker** on privacy grounds and leans heavily on his union.
Fast AGI **alarms** him because the thinking half of his job goes while the loan is still big.
With ten years he'd clear the debt and finally learn **hands-on procedures** from his senior partner.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the thinking part of his job goes while he still has the loan and no savings.
whatWouldHelp: A law that a doctor **signs off** every diagnosis, plus **loan relief** if his hours are cut.
